title: EVA Air to Launch Nonstop Taipei–Delhi Flights in December, Targeting India-US Transit Market
excerpt: Taiwan's second-largest carrier plans to connect Delhi to its North American network of 10 cities, offering one-stop routes for Indian tech professionals heading to Silicon Valley.
body:
• EVA Air plans to launch nonstop flights between Taipei and Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport starting December 1, 2026, subject to regulatory approval.
  • The route is designed to tap India-to-North America transit traffic, with early morning connections from Taipei to Los Angeles, Seattle, San Francisco, and seven other US and Canadian cities.
  • EVA Air President Sun Chia-ming said the airline will specifically target Indian software engineers working in Silicon Valley.
  • The new service puts EVA Air in direct competition with Cathay Pacific and Singapore Airlines in the South Asia–North America transit corridor.

Delhi Gets a New Gateway to North America

EVA Air, one of Taiwan's two major international carriers, has filed an application to operate nonstop flights between Taipei Taoyuan International Airport and Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport, with services expected to begin on December 1, 2026.

EVA Air President Sun Chia-ming confirmed the plans while in Washington, D.C., following the airline's recent launch of direct flights to the US capital. Speaking to reporters, Sun said Delhi's strategic location makes it an ideal gateway for passengers travelling between South Asia and North America.

"Delhi's strategic position as a link between North America and South Asia makes it a key route for us. We plan to target Indian software engineers working in Silicon Valley with this new service."

— Sun Chia-ming, President, EVA Air

How the Connections Work

The Delhi route is not just about the Taipei-Delhi leg. EVA Air's real pitch is connectivity. The airline operates early morning departures from Taipei to major US gateways including Los Angeles, Seattle, San Francisco, New York, Chicago, and Houston. A passenger flying from Delhi would arrive in Taipei and connect onward to North America — a one-stop journey through a Star Alliance hub.

EVA Air currently serves 10 destinations across North America with 98 weekly round-trip flights, more than the combined North American operations of fellow Taiwanese carriers China Airlines and Starlux Airlines. North America accounts for approximately 40% of EVA Air's passenger revenue and 70% of its cargo revenue, according to Sun.

With Taiwan's domestic market limited to 23 million people, international transit traffic is critical for the airline's growth strategy. The Delhi route would extend that funnel into one of the world's fastest-growing aviation markets.

Competing for the India Corridor

The Taipei-Delhi launch puts EVA Air squarely in competition with established transit carriers on the India-North America corridor. Cathay Pacific routes passengers through Hong Kong, Singapore Airlines through Changi, and several Gulf carriers offer one-stop options through Dubai and Doha.

EVA Air's advantage lies in its dense US network and the relatively short transit time through Taipei. For passengers headed to West Coast destinations, the Taipei routing can shave hours off alternatives via the Middle East.

The airline previously operated flights to Mumbai but has since discontinued that route. Delhi will be its sole Indian destination when services begin, according to Wikipedia's list of EVA Air destinations, which already shows the December 1 launch date.

What Indian Travellers Should Know

EVA Air is a member of the Star Alliance, which means frequent flyer benefits extend across partner airlines including Air India, United Airlines, and Lufthansa. The airline is consistently ranked among the world's safest and best-service carriers — it placed in Airline Ratings' top tier for 2026.

Pricing and schedule details have not been announced, but based on EVA Air's existing long-haul fare structure, the Taipei-Delhi route is expected to be competitively priced against Gulf carrier alternatives, particularly for passengers connecting to the US West Coast.

For Indians in the US — especially the large tech workforce in the Bay Area and Seattle — the new route offers a Pacific routing alternative that avoids the long westbound haul through Europe or the Gulf. It also opens up Taipei itself as a leisure destination, one that has seen growing interest from Indian travellers in recent years.
